chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from al-Nadr, from 'Asim ibn Humayd, from Abi Basir al-Makfuf, who said:
I asked Aba 'Abdillah عليه السلام about the fasting person: when does food become forbidden for him?

He said: When the dawn is like the white Qibtiyyah cloth. I said: Then when does the salat (prayer) become permissible? He said: When it is like that. So I said: Am I not within a time, from that hour until the sun rises? He said: No, we only count that as the prayer of children.
Then he said: A man was not considered praiseworthy if he were to perform salat (prayer) in the mosque and then return and wake his family and children.

key_terms.الصَّلَاةُ: salat (prayer), here specifically the Fajr prayer
key_terms.الطَّعَامُ: food, whose consumption becomes forbidden at dawn for fasting
key_terms.الْفَجْرُ: dawn, marking the onset of fasting and Fajr salat (prayer)
key_terms.الْقُبْطِيَّةِ الْبَيْضَاءِ: the white Qibtiyyah cloth, used here as a simile for the appearance of dawn
key_terms.صَلَاةَ الصِّبْيَانِ: the prayer of children, referring here to an overly early performance before the proper time

ai.seo_question: When does food become forbidden for the fasting person, and when does the time of Fajr salat (prayer) begin?
ai.summary: This hadith explains the beginning of the time when eating becomes forbidden for the fasting person and when Fajr salat (prayer) becomes due, tying both to the appearance of true dawn. It also indicates disapproval of praying so early that one returns from the mosque only to awaken his family and children afterward.
